title: A Promise with No Audience
subtitle: Jasmine After Rain · Chapter 36 of 40
content:
The balcony had one good chair and two people who wanted it.

Iroh discovered this at sunset and behaved as though we had reached an international crisis.

"I insist you sit," he said.

"I insist we stop pretending this chair is a throne."

"It has excellent support."

"It has a splinter."

He looked at the seat, then at me.

"An imperfection in the kingdom."

I laughed and sat on the low bench beside the railing instead. It was cooler there. The city had quieted after the tea rush, though I could still hear the last delivery cart turning into the lane.

Iroh joined me with two cups.

We had planned a private evening. No festival, no lesson, no public speech. He had asked whether we could talk about what we wanted next, and I'd agreed before either of us could invent a reason to put it off.

He set his cup down carefully.

"Are you nervous?" I asked.

"Very."

"About talking to me?"

"About speaking as though I know the future."

"You don't have to."

He considered.

"I suppose I was hoping for an impressive answer."

"I've already heard your impressive answers. I'd like a true one."

The balcony went quiet.

I could smell the evening's last jasmine steeping downstairs. The shutters had been repaired that morning. Someone had replaced a loose nail in the rail and left the spare on the sill, where Iroh kept moving it out of sight and forgetting to put it away.

"I want you to come back," he said at last.

"I plan to."

"That was not a demand. I know you have other people you love."

"I know you know."

He took a breath.

"I sometimes feel foolish for wanting a promise when we've already spoken plainly."

"Wanting reassurance isn't foolish. What kind of promise?"

He looked toward the lane.

"A morning. Perhaps Thursday. The kind of ordinary plan we can keep even when the rest of our worlds insist on being complicated."

I smiled.

"Thursday morning I have to be at Moonroot."

His face fell before he could stop it.

"Friday?"

I checked the small calendar tucked in my notebook.

"Friday works. I can come through the Threadway in the afternoon and stay for breakfast the next day."

He looked surprised.

"You can simply choose that?"

"Yes. So can you. You can tell me if you need to change it."

We had been explicit about my being ethically non-monogamous and preferring polyamory. It had never meant I could offer everybody every hour. It meant the opposite: telling the truth about the hours I actually had, letting people decide whether they wanted to share them, and hearing their disappointment without trying to make it disappear.

Iroh leaned against the rail.

"And what if I have an errand for Zuko that takes longer than expected?"

"Tell me. We'll choose another day. I might be disappointed, but that doesn't mean you've failed a test."

He nodded slowly.

"What if I would rather not entertain the Fire Lord's next messenger at all?"

"Then you can say the shop is closed and reply tomorrow."

He laughed.

"I may have to practice that sentence."

"Write it down."

He pulled a scrap of paper from his sleeve and wrote: *I will answer tomorrow.*

I stared.

"Do you carry blank paper for every possible piece of advice?"

"Only the important ones."

I took the pencil and added: *Unless the kitchen is on fire.*

"An excellent amendment," he said solemnly.

Mina knocked at the balcony door just then.

"I heard that," she said. "The kitchen is not on fire. But the storage shelf still needs a carpenter's estimate. Shall I call one tomorrow?"

"Please," Iroh answered. "And do not give them my personal number for evening visits."

Mina lifted an eyebrow.

"Progress."

When she had gone, Iroh looked pleased with himself.

"I have made a boundary."

"Very impressive."

"I should have the chair repaired in celebration."

"After you get the estimate."

He groaned theatrically.

The wind turned colder. He took the extra shawl from the bench and held it toward me.

"May I?"

"Yes."

He set it around my shoulders without treating it as a reason to pull me into his lap. I leaned into him a moment later because I wanted to.

"What do you want from us?" he asked.

I took longer to answer than I'd expected.

"Not just comfort," I said. "I want to be able to disagree with you. To laugh when your advice is terrible. To go home to another person without you pretending that makes this less real."

His hand tightened once, then relaxed.

"And I want to be told when a plan changes," he said. "Not every private detail. Just what affects the time we have chosen."

"That's fair."

He smiled.

"We make very unpoetic promises."

"Good. Poetry makes terrible calendars."

We kissed at the balcony door, slowly enough that I could feel him smile before I pulled back. The warmth between us didn't require an audience or a vow no one could revise.

He asked whether I'd like to stay the night. I said yes. We put the cups away, checked the shutters, and closed the door.

On Friday, a small card waited beside the breakfast table: *Reserved for two people who asked.*

Underneath it, in smaller handwriting, Mina had added: *Please return the chair to the carpenter.*

I laughed so hard I had to sit down.

Iroh poured the tea and looked thoroughly delighted.
